subject: Mixed (Real Weightage)
description: 100 questions following the real PGP-CET 2025 subject weightage. Mix: 38 easy / 51 medium / 11 hard. Every question cites its source.

questions.question: A 'Bankart lesion' of the shoulder refers to:

options.A: Detachment of the anteroinferior labrum, commonly occurring with traumatic anterior dislocation
options.B: A tear confined strictly to the superior labrum (10 to 2 o'clock position)
options.C: A rotator cuff tear with no labral involvement
options.D: A fracture of the greater tuberosity

questions.explanation: A Bankart lesion is a tear of the anteroinferior labrum (roughly the 3 to 7 o'clock position in the right shoulder), most commonly occurring with a traumatic anterior dislocation, also compromising the stability of the inferior glenohumeral ligament.
questions.sourceBook: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 5: Shoulder — Tests for Labral Tears
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: 'Rusty' coloured sputum is classically associated with infection by which organism?

options.B: Pneumococcus

questions.explanation: Rusty-coloured sputum is a classic finding associated with pneumococcal infection (typical lobar pneumonia), whereas dark green/brown sputum suggests Pseudomonas, and 'red-currant jelly' sputum suggests Klebsiella.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.sourceChapter: Assessment — Sputum
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: When faradic-type current is applied directly over an innervated muscle, maximum contraction response is generally obtained by stimulating at the:

options.B: Motor point — where the main nerve enters the muscle (or, for deep muscles, where it emerges from under more superficial muscles)
options.C: Muscle belly midpoint, regardless of nerve entry

questions.explanation: The motor point — the point at which the main nerve supply enters the muscle, or for deeply placed muscles, the point where the nerve emerges from under overlying superficial muscles — is where maximum contraction response is typically obtained with electrical stimulation.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle — Effects of Nerve Stimulation
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: Derealisation and depersonalisation, when they occur as anxiety symptoms, are classified under which category of psychological symptoms?

options.B: Perceptual symptoms

questions.explanation: Derealisation and depersonalisation are classified as perceptual symptoms of anxiety, distinct from cognitive symptoms (poor concentration, distractibility), affective symptoms (fearfulness, apprehension), and physical/motoric symptoms (tremors, restlessness).
questions.sourceBook: Ahuja, A Short Textbook of Psychiatry
questions.sourceChapter: Neurotic, Stress-related and Somatoform Disorders — Anxiety Disorder, Symptoms
questions.subject: Psychiatry

questions.question: SBAR, a structured communication tool used for handovers and referrals, stands for:

options.B: Symptoms, Blood tests, Allergies, Review

questions.explanation: SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) is a structured communication framework recommended for handovers and referrals, increasing the amount of relevant clinical information communicated in a short time.
questions.sourceBook: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Clinical Decision Making — Effective Team Communication
questions.subject: Medicine

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: A faradic-type current is best defined as:

options.B: A short-duration interrupted direct current with a pulse duration of 0.1-1 ms and a frequency of 50-100 Hz
options.C: A current only used for denervated muscle
options.D: A current with pulse durations always exceeding 100 ms

questions.explanation: A faradic-type current is a short-duration interrupted direct current with a pulse duration of 0.1-1 ms and a frequency of 50-100 Hz — modern electronic stimulators reproduce the same physiological effects as the original faradic coil, just via a different circuit mechanism.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle — Faradic-Type Current
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: Stridor is often mistakenly called 'wheeze' by patients, but it actually indicates:

options.B: Pleural effusion

questions.explanation: Stridor is the sound produced by upper airway obstruction and is often mistakenly labelled 'wheeze' by patients, though true wheeze arises from turbulent airflow through narrowed lower airways — an important clinical distinction.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.sourceChapter: Assessment — Wheeze
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: A daily, chronic productive cough is described as a fundamental feature of which conditions?

options.B: Chronic bronchitis and bronchiectasis

questions.explanation: A chronic productive cough occurring every day is a fundamental feature of chronic bronchitis and bronchiectasis, whereas interstitial lung disease is characteristically associated with a persistent DRY cough.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.sourceChapter: Assessment — Cough
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: Which two special tests are classically used to assess for a meniscal injury of the knee?

options.B: Lachman test and pivot shift test
options.C: Clarke's sign and the Q-angle measurement
options.D: Noble compression test and Ober's test

questions.explanation: The McMurray test and Apley's (compression/distraction) test are the classic special tests for meniscal injury of the knee, alongside the 'bounce home' test.
questions.sourceBook: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 12: Knee — Special Tests Commonly Performed on the Knee
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: The hook-like projection near the base of which carpal bone gives attachment to the flexor retinaculum?

options.B: Trapezium

questions.explanation: The hamate is wedge-shaped with a hook projecting from the distal part of its palmar surface; the tip of the hook gives attachment to the flexor retinaculum, and its medial side gives origin to flexor digiti minimi and opponens digiti minimi.
questions.sourceBook: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy — Upper Limb
questions.sourceChapter: Bones of the Upper Limb — Carpal Bones
questions.subject: Anatomy

questions.question: The 'ceiling effect' of manual muscle testing refers to which limitation of the technique?

options.A: It cannot detect any degree of weakness whatsoever
options.B: A wide range of actual muscle force can all be labeled Grade 5 (Normal), masking real strength differences among people graded 'normal'
options.C: It systematically overestimates weakness in older adults
options.D: It is not valid for testing lower-extremity muscles

questions.explanation: Studies comparing MMT to hand-held dynamometry found knee extension forces ranging roughly from 85 to over 800 Newtons all classified as Grade 5 (Normal) by break testing. This 'ceiling effect' means MMT loses the ability to distinguish real strength differences once a muscle is already strong, so it is not recommended as a measure of progress above Grade 3.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels and Worthingham's Muscle Testing, 9th ed.
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 2: Relevance and Limitations of Manual Muscle Testing
questions.subject: Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills

questions.question: According to the New York Heart Association (NYHA) classification of breathlessness, a patient who becomes symptomatic with mild exertion such as bathing or dressing falls into which class?

options.B: Class II

questions.explanation: NYHA Class III describes symptoms occurring with mild exertion (e.g. bathing, showering, dressing). Class I is asymptomatic except with severe exertion, Class II is symptomatic with ordinary activity (e.g. walking upstairs), and Class IV is symptomatic even at rest.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.sourceChapter: Assessment — Breathlessness Classification
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: Hughston's posteromedial drawer sign is performed with the patient supine, knee flexed 80-90°, hip flexed 45°, and the foot slightly medially rotated. A positive test (excessive posterior movement/rotation of the medial tibia) is most indicative of injury to which primary structure?

options.B: Posterior cruciate ligament (along with posteromedial supporting structures)

questions.explanation: A positive Hughston's posteromedial drawer sign indicates injury to the posterior cruciate ligament, along with possible involvement of the posterior oblique ligament, medial collateral ligament, semimembranosus, and posteromedial capsule — it tests for posteromedial rotary instability of the knee.
questions.sourceBook: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 12: Knee — Ligament Stability, Posteromedial and Posterolateral Drawer Sign
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: Which of the following is described as a powerful, independent risk factor for stroke, associated with roughly a fivefold increase in risk?

options.B: Seasonal allergies

questions.explanation: Atrial fibrillation is described as a powerful risk factor for stroke, associated with approximately a fivefold increase in stroke risk, due to its potential to generate cardiac emboli.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 15: Stroke — Risk Factors and Stroke Prevention
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: While a rising current initiates an impulse most effectively at the cathode, a FALL in current (when it occurs) is more effective at initiating an impulse at which electrode?

options.B: The anode
options.C: Neither electrode is affected by a falling current

questions.explanation: A fall in current is less effective overall at initiating an impulse than a rise, but when it does have an effect, it is the anode side of the nerve that is affected — so the anode produces greater stimulation than the cathode specifically in response to a falling current, the reverse of the pattern seen with a rising current.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle — Accommodation
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: In the tibial external rotation (Dial) test, if the tibia rotates MORE at 90° of knee flexion than at 30°, this pattern most likely indicates injury to:

options.A: Only the popliteus corner (isolated posterolateral injury)
options.B: Both the popliteus corner AND the posterior cruciate ligament
options.C: The anterior cruciate ligament in isolation

questions.explanation: In the Dial test, if the tibia rotates less at 90° than at 30°, an isolated posterolateral (popliteus corner) injury is more likely. If it rotates MORE at 90° than at 30°, combined injury to both the popliteus corner and the posterior cruciate ligament is more likely.
questions.sourceBook: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 12: Knee — Tibial External Rotation (Dial) Test
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: Closed-chain exercise is best described as exercise performed:

options.A: In a nonweight-bearing position with the distal segment moving freely
options.B: In a weight-bearing position where the body moves over a fixed distal segment
options.C: Only using free weights, never body weight

questions.explanation: Closed-chain exercise is performed in a weight-bearing position, where the body moves over a relatively fixed distal segment (e.g. the foot on the ground during a squat). Open-chain exercise, by contrast, is performed nonweight-bearing, with the distal segment (hand or foot) moving freely.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 6: Resistance Exercise — Position for Exercise
questions.subject: Kinesio Therapeutics

questions.question: The resting membrane potential is conventionally written with a minus sign because:

options.A: It signifies the inside of the cell is negative relative to the outside
options.B: It signifies the outside of the cell is negative relative to the inside
options.C: The sign is arbitrary and carries no physiological meaning
options.D: It indicates the cell is in the process of depolarising

questions.explanation: The resting membrane potential is written with a minus sign to indicate that, at rest, the interior of the cell is electrically negative relative to the exterior — its magnitude varies by tissue, typically ranging from about -10 mV to -100 mV.
questions.sourceBook: AK Jain, Physiology
questions.sourceChapter: The Membrane Potentials — Resting Membrane Potential
questions.subject: Physiology

questions.question: The Hawkins-Kennedy impingement test involves forward flexing the arm to 90° and then forcibly:

options.B: Laterally rotating the shoulder only

questions.explanation: In the Hawkins-Kennedy test, the examiner forward flexes the arm to 90° and then forcibly medially rotates the shoulder, pushing the supraspinatus tendon against the coracoacromial ligament and coracoid process — pain indicates a positive test for supraspinatus tendinosis or impingement.
questions.sourceBook: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 5: Shoulder — Hawkins-Kennedy Impingement Test
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: 'Passive flexibility' (passive range of motion) is best described as:

options.A: The degree to which an active muscle contraction moves a joint through its available range
options.B: The degree to which a body segment can be moved through its available range by an external force, without the patient contracting the muscle themselves
options.C: The absolute maximum range any joint could reach under general anesthesia
options.D: A measure of muscular endurance during repeated contractions

questions.explanation: Passive flexibility depends on the extensibility of the muscles and connective tissues crossing a joint. It is a prerequisite for, but does not guarantee, dynamic (active) flexibility — which instead depends on the patient's own active muscle contraction moving the segment.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 4: Stretching for Impaired Mobility — Definition of Terms
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Exercise Therapy

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT listed among the basic measurements used in epidemiology?

options.B: Measurement of morbidity
options.D: Measurement of a patient's personal income

questions.explanation: Basic epidemiological measurements include mortality, morbidity, disability, natality, presence/absence/distribution of disease characteristics, medical needs and health service utilisation, environmental factors, and demographic variables — personal income is not one of the standard categories listed, though socioeconomic status may be studied as a demographic variable.
questions.sourceBook: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Epidemiology and Epidemiologic Methods — Basic Measurements in Epidemiology
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Community Health

questions.question: Vitamin B6 collectively refers to which three related pyridine-derivative compounds?

options.B: Thiamine, riboflavin, and niacin

questions.explanation: Vitamin B6 collectively represents three related pyridine-derivative compounds — pyridoxine (a primary alcohol form), pyridoxal (an aldehyde form), and pyridoxamine (an amine form) — which can interconvert, and are together known as the vitamers of B6.
questions.sourceBook: Satyanarayana, Biochemistry
questions.sourceChapter: Vitamins — Vitamin B6, Chemistry
questions.subject: Biochemistry

questions.question: When multiple muscle groups are exercised in a single session, the recommended order is generally:

options.A: Small muscle groups before large muscle groups, single-joint before multi-joint exercises
options.B: Large muscle groups before small muscle groups, and multi-joint exercises before single-joint exercises
options.C: Order makes no difference to fatigue or training effect
options.D: Lower intensity exercises should always precede higher intensity ones, regardless of warm-up

questions.explanation: The recommended exercise order is large muscle groups before small muscle groups, and multi-joint exercises before single-joint exercises, with higher-intensity exercises performed before lower-intensity ones after an appropriate warm-up.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 6: Resistance Exercise — Exercise Order
questions.subject: Kinesio Therapeutics

questions.question: A SLAP lesion (Superior Labrum, Anterior and Posterior) involves detachment of the labrum at approximately which clock-face position, and is often caused by what mechanism?

options.A: 10 to 2 o'clock position; often from a FOOSH injury or during deceleration in throwing
options.B: 3 to 7 o'clock position; only from anterior dislocation
options.C: 6 o'clock position exclusively; from a direct blow to the shoulder
options.D: SLAP lesions never have an identifiable mechanism

questions.explanation: A SLAP lesion involves detachment of the labrum from roughly the 10 to 2 o'clock position, often occurring from a FOOSH (fall on outstretched hand) injury or during the deceleration phase of throwing; if the biceps tendon also detaches, the superior glenohumeral ligament support is lost and the shoulder becomes unstable.
questions.sourceBook: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 5: Shoulder — Tests for Labral Tears
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: How is a 'strain' distinguished from a 'sprain' in soft tissue injury terminology?

options.A: A strain refers to some degree of disruption of the musculotendinous unit; a sprain refers specifically to injury of a ligament, joint capsule, or similar structure
options.B: The two terms are completely interchangeable with no distinction
options.C: A strain is always more severe than any sprain
options.D: A sprain only ever occurs in muscle, never in ligaments

questions.explanation: A strain refers to overstretching/overuse causing some degree of disruption of the musculotendinous unit, tending to be less severe. A sprain refers to more severe stress, stretch, or tear of soft tissues such as a joint capsule, ligament, or tendon — graded as first (mild), second (moderate), or third (severe) degree.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 10: Soft Tissue Injury, Repair, and Management — Soft Tissue Lesions
questions.subject: Kinesio Therapeutics

questions.question: Angina pectoris from myocardial ischaemia is classically described as:

options.A: A sharp, localized pain that worsens specifically on inspiration
options.B: A dull, central, retrosternal gripping or band-like sensation that may radiate to the arm, neck, or jaw
options.C: A superficial pain reproduced by chest wall palpation
options.D: A pain confined strictly to the left shoulder with no central component

questions.explanation: Angina pectoris characteristically produces a dull, central, retrosternal gripping or band-like sensation, which may radiate to either arm, the neck, or the jaw — quite distinct from the sharp, localized, movement/palpation-related pain of musculoskeletal chest pain.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.sourceChapter: Assessment — Chest Pain
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: An umbilical hernia in an infant, caused by incomplete closure of the umbilical ring, most commonly:

options.B: Resolves spontaneously by around 4 years of age
options.C: Always requires surgical repair within the first month of life
options.D: Is a surgical emergency due to a very high incarceration rate

questions.explanation: Umbilical hernias are common in infants and most resolve spontaneously by around 4 years of age, with incarceration being very rare — unlike supraumbilical hernias, which do not close on their own and are repaired around the same age.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Paediatric Surgery — Midline Hernias
questions.subject: General Surgery & Orthopedics

questions.question: At rest, the cell membrane is:

options.A: Freely permeable to Na+ but impermeable to K+
options.B: Effectively impermeable (or only moderately permeable) to Na+, but freely permeable to K+ and Cl-
options.C: Equally permeable to Na+ and K+
options.D: Impermeable to all ions including K+ and Cl-

questions.explanation: At rest, the cell membrane is effectively impermeable (or only moderately permeable) to Na+, while being freely permeable to K+ and Cl- — K+ permeability is roughly 50-100 times greater than Na+ permeability, which is fundamental to the genesis of the resting membrane potential.
questions.sourceBook: AK Jain, Physiology
questions.sourceChapter: The Membrane Potentials — Introduction
questions.subject: Physiology

questions.question: Regarding physical activity and stroke risk, which finding is reported?

options.A: Moderate to vigorous exercise is associated with about a 35% reduction in stroke risk, while light exercise (walking) does not show the same benefit
options.B: Exercise of any intensity has no effect on stroke risk whatsoever
options.C: Only vigorous exercise increases stroke risk
options.D: Light walking provides the greatest protective benefit, more than vigorous exercise

questions.explanation: Moderate to vigorous physical activity is associated with an overall 35% reduction in stroke risk, whereas light exercise such as walking alone does not appear to confer the same degree of protective benefit.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 15: Stroke — Risk Factors and Stroke Prevention
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: In manual muscle testing, the 'break test' is best described as:

options.A: Applying resistance throughout an actively moving joint to see when motion ceases
options.B: Bringing the part to the end of its available range and asking the patient to hold that position while the therapist tries to force ('break') it out of position
options.C: Passively moving a joint until tissue resistance is felt
options.D: Timing how long a muscle can sustain a maximal isometric hold

questions.explanation: The break test — the most commonly used MMT procedure — has the patient hold the end-range test position while the therapist applies gradually increasing resistance, attempting to 'break' the hold. The alternative 'active resistance test' (resisting throughout the motion) requires more skill and is not generally recommended because results are often equivocal.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels and Worthingham's Muscle Testing, 9th ed.
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 1: Principles of Manual Muscle Testing
questions.subject: Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills

questions.question: Continuous Passive Motion (CPM) is best described as:

options.A: An exercise in which the patient actively moves a joint against resistance
options.B: A mechanical device that moves a joint slowly and continuously through a controlled range of motion, without effort from the patient
options.C: A manual stretching technique applied by the therapist at end-range
options.D: A functional movement pattern combining several joints at once

questions.explanation: CPM refers specifically to a mechanical device that passively and continuously moves a joint through a set arc of motion, developed following Robert Salter's research into the healing benefits of continual passive movement on joint tissue.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 3: Range of Motion — Continuous Passive Motion
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Exercise Therapy

questions.question: On the Glasgow Coma Scale, what is the maximum total score, and what does it represent?

options.B: 15, representing a fully alert, orientated patient

questions.explanation: The Glasgow Coma Scale has a maximum total score of 15 (best possible — eye opening 4, verbal response 5, motor response 6), representing full alertness, and a minimum score of 3, representing the deepest level of unresponsiveness.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.sourceChapter: Assessment — Objective Assessment, Coma Scale
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: In a practical setup for stimulating the quadriceps with a faradic-type current, where is the indifferent (larger) electrode typically placed, per Clayton's described technique?

options.A: Over the femoral nerve in the femoral triangle
options.B: Directly over the motor points of the quadriceps only, with no separate indifferent electrode

questions.explanation: In the classic technique for faradic stimulation of the quadriceps, one electrode and pad is placed over the femoral nerve in the femoral triangle and secured with a sandbag or bandage, while the other (active) electrode pad is placed across the motor points of the quadriceps.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Stimulation of Muscle Groups — Quadriceps
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: On manual muscle testing (MMT), a muscle completes the full available range of motion against gravity alone, but the motion breaks as soon as any additional manual resistance is applied, however mild. What grade should this muscle receive?

options.B: Grade 4 (Good)

questions.explanation: Grade 3 (Fair) is an objective grade: the muscle can complete full range of motion against gravity, but cannot tolerate any added resistance without breaking. Grade 4 requires the muscle to also withstand considerable, though submaximal, resistance.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels and Worthingham's Muscle Testing, 9th ed.
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 1: Principles of Manual Muscle Testing
questions.subject: Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills

questions.question: Occlusion of a posterior cerebral artery (PCA), affecting the occipital lobe, characteristically produces:

options.B: Complete bilateral blindness in every case
options.D: Pure motor weakness with no sensory or visual involvement

questions.explanation: The PCA supplies the occipital lobe (primary visual cortex); occlusion produces contralateral homonymous hemianopsia. Bilateral PCA occlusion can cause cortical blindness, but this is not the typical single-vessel presentation.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 15: Stroke — Posterior Cerebral Artery Syndrome
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: Middle Cerebral Artery (MCA) syndrome, the most common site of occlusion in stroke, classically produces contralateral weakness and sensory loss most affecting:

options.A: The lower extremity, sparing the face and upper extremity
options.B: The face and upper extremity, with relative sparing of the lower extremity

questions.explanation: MCA syndrome classically produces contralateral spastic hemiparesis and sensory loss of the face, upper extremity, and lower extremity, with the face and upper extremity more affected than the lower extremity — the MCA is also the most common site of stroke occlusion overall.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 15: Stroke — Middle Cerebral Artery Syndrome
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: The circle of Willis is clinically important in stroke because it:

options.A: Has no role in cerebral perfusion at all
options.B: Provides a collateral circulatory network that can help maintain blood flow if one contributing artery is occluded proximally
options.C: Is located exclusively in the spinal cord

questions.explanation: The circle of Willis connects the anterior and posterior cerebral circulations via communicating arteries, providing collateral blood flow. This is why occlusion proximal to the anterior or posterior communicating arteries often produces relatively minimal deficits — perfusion can be partly maintained from the other side.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 15: Stroke — Vascular Syndromes
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: A child injured by a bicycle handlebar to the abdomen is classically at risk of injury to which structures?

options.B: Pancreatic, duodenal, mesenteric, or liver trauma
options.C: The small intestine or lumbar spine only
options.D: Severe crush injury to the chest exclusively

questions.explanation: Handlebar injuries classically cause focal, high-pressure blunt trauma to the upper abdomen, putting the pancreas, duodenum, mesentery, or liver at risk — distinct from lap belt injuries (small intestine/lumbar spine) or straddle injuries (urethra/pelvis).
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Paediatric Surgery — Paediatric Trauma, Patterns of Injury
questions.subject: General Surgery & Orthopedics

questions.question: The World Health Organization defines a 'zoonosis' as:

options.A: Any infection that only ever affects animals, never humans
options.B: A disease or infection that is naturally transmissible from vertebrate animals to humans
options.C: An infection transmitted exclusively via insect vectors
options.D: A disease found only in tropical climates

questions.explanation: The WHO defines a zoonosis as a disease or infection naturally transmissible from vertebrate animals to humans. Infected animals may be asymptomatic, and some zoonoses (e.g. Q fever, Ebola) can then spread onward between humans, causing secondary disease.
questions.sourceBook: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Epidemiology of Infection — Reservoirs of Infection
questions.subject: Medicine

questions.question: Caseous necrosis, with its characteristic 'cheese-like' gross appearance, is classically found in the centre of which type of lesion?

options.B: Simple traumatic bruising

questions.explanation: Caseous necrosis is found classically in the centre of tuberculous foci — combining features of both coagulative and liquefactive necrosis — with surrounding granulomatous inflammation (epithelioid cells, Langhans' giant cells, and a peripheral lymphocyte mantle).
questions.sourceBook: Harsh Mohan, Textbook of Pathology
questions.sourceChapter: Cell Injury, Cellular Adaptations and Cellular Ageing — Caseous Necrosis
questions.subject: Pathology & Microbiology

questions.question: During the ACUTE (inflammatory) stage of tissue healing, pain on range of motion testing is typically experienced:

options.A: Only after full range has been achieved, with no resistance
options.B: BEFORE tissue resistance is encountered, with guarding before completion of range
options.C: Never — the acute stage is always painless
options.D: Only during the chronic stage, not the acute stage

questions.explanation: In the acute (inflammatory) stage, pain occurs BEFORE tissue resistance is encountered during ROM testing, and the patient typically guards against the motion before the available range is completed — contrasted with the subacute stage (pain synchronous with resistance) and chronic stage (pain only after resistance, at end-range).
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 10: Soft Tissue Injury, Repair, and Management — Stages of Inflammation and Repair
questions.subject: Kinesio Therapeutics

questions.question: The Neer impingement test involves the examiner passively and forcibly elevating the patient's medially-rotated arm in the scapular plane. A positive test (pain) is most indicative of an overuse injury to which structure?

options.A: The supraspinatus muscle (and sometimes the biceps tendon)
options.B: The ulnar nerve

questions.explanation: The Neer impingement test causes 'jamming' of the greater tuberosity against the anteroinferior border of the acromion; a positive test (reproducing pain) is indicative of an overuse injury to the supraspinatus muscle, and sometimes the biceps tendon.
questions.sourceBook: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 5: Shoulder — Common Shoulder Impingement Tests, Neer Impingement Test
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: Inguinal hernias in children are almost always caused by:

options.A: A direct defect in the abdominal wall muscles
options.B: A patent processus vaginalis (indirect hernia)

questions.explanation: Inguinal hernias in children are almost always indirect, caused by failure of the processus vaginalis (the tongue of peritoneum that precedes testicular descent) to obliterate after birth.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Paediatric Surgery — Inguinal Hernias
questions.subject: General Surgery & Orthopedics

questions.question: A 'pseudomyostatic' (apparent) contracture, as distinguished from a true myostatic contracture, is primarily caused by:

options.A: An actual reduction in the number of sarcomeres arranged in series within the muscle
options.B: Hypertonicity such as spasticity or rigidity following a CNS lesion, which can be temporarily reduced with neuromuscular inhibition techniques
options.D: Replacement of normal muscle tissue with fibrotic scar tissue

questions.explanation: Unlike a true myostatic contracture (adaptive shortening of the muscle-tendon unit itself with no specific muscle pathology), a pseudomyostatic contracture results from ongoing hypertonicity, muscle spasm, or pain — the muscle only appears shortened, and full passive elongation becomes possible again once inhibition techniques temporarily reduce that muscle tension.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 4: Stretching for Impaired Mobility — Types of Contracture
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Exercise Therapy

questions.question: Unintentional weight loss of more than what percentage of body weight over the preceding 6 months is considered a good indicator of poor prognosis?

options.D: Weight loss is never prognostically significant

questions.explanation: Unintentional weight loss of more than 10% of a patient's body weight over the preceding 6 months is considered a good prognostic indicator of poor outcome.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Nutritional Assessment — Body Weight and Anthropometry
questions.subject: General Surgery & Orthopedics

questions.question: A patient's gluteus medius is graded 4 (Good) on manual muscle testing. Which functional finding is consistent with this grade, per Daniels and Worthingham's discussion of why 'Good' is not always good enough?

options.A: Completely normal, symmetric gait with no compensation
options.B: A positive Trendelenburg sign during single-leg stance
options.C: Complete inability to abduct the hip against gravity
options.D: No palpable or visible muscle contraction at all

questions.explanation: Even a 'Good' (Grade 4) gluteus medius can be functionally inadequate — a positive Trendelenburg sign (contralateral pelvic drop in single-leg stance) can still appear, illustrating the gap between a manual muscle grade and real functional performance.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels and Worthingham's Muscle Testing, 9th ed.
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 1: Principles of Manual Muscle Testing
questions.subject: Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: 'Accommodation' in nerve physiology refers to the phenomenon whereby:

options.A: A nerve becomes permanently unresponsive after any stimulation
options.B: The nerve adapts to a constant current over time, so that an unvarying (unchanging) current becomes ineffective at initiating an impulse
options.C: Muscle fibres physically move position to avoid the electrode
options.D: Only denervated muscle can show accommodation

questions.explanation: Accommodation is the nerve's adaptation to a constant, unvarying current flow through a mechanism not fully understood — as a result, a current that does not change is not effective at initiating a nerve impulse, which is why intermittent or varying currents are needed for electrical stimulation.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle — Accommodation
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: The reddish vaginal discharge seen in the first 1-4 days after delivery is called:

options.B: Lochia serosa

questions.explanation: Lochia progresses through three stages by colour: lochia rubra (red, days 1-4), lochia serosa (yellowish/pink/pale brownish, days 5-9), and lochia alba (pale white, days 10-15).
questions.sourceBook: Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics
questions.sourceChapter: Normal Puerperium — Lochia
questions.subject: OBGY

questions.question: According to the framework for 'asking questions' in epidemiology, which of the following is a question 'related to health action' rather than 'related to health events'?

options.B: What resources are required, and how are activities to be organized?

questions.explanation: Questions like 'what is the event', 'where/when did it happen', and 'who is affected' are related to health events. Questions about what resources are required and how activities should be organized fall under questions related to health action — what should be done about the problem.
questions.sourceBook: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Epidemiology and Epidemiologic Methods — Asking Questions
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Community Health

questions.question: Approximately 60-75% of the body's total platelet pool circulates in the blood at any time; where is most of the remainder stored?

options.B: The liver

questions.explanation: The spleen acts as a reservoir of platelets, holding most of the platelets not currently in general circulation — this is why splenectomy or splenic contraction (e.g. from epinephrine or stress) can significantly alter the circulating platelet count.
questions.sourceBook: AK Jain, Physiology
questions.sourceChapter: Platelets or Thrombocytes — Count and Variations
questions.subject: Physiology

questions.question: When the velocity of a limb movement is held constant by a rate-controlling device during exercise, this is referred to as:

options.B: Isokinetic contraction

questions.explanation: An isokinetic contraction is one where the velocity of limb movement is held constant by a rate-controlling device (an isokinetic dynamometer), distinguishing it from standard dynamic (isotonic) exercise where velocity is not controlled.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 6: Resistance Exercise — Type of Muscle Contraction
questions.subject: Kinesio Therapeutics

questions.question: The Noble compression test is used to assess for which condition?

options.B: Meniscal tear

questions.explanation: The Noble compression test is used to assess for iliotibial band friction syndrome, a common cause of lateral knee pain particularly in runners.
questions.sourceBook: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 12: Knee — Special Tests Commonly Performed on the Knee
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: Inanimate objects such as door handles, water taps, and ultrasound probes that bridge transmission of infection between hosts are called:

options.B: Fomites

questions.explanation: Fomites are inanimate objects (door handles, water taps, medical equipment) that can bridge transmission of infection between an infected source and a susceptible host, and are particularly associated with health care-associated infection. Vectors, by contrast, are animate carriers (e.g. mosquitoes, fleas).
questions.sourceBook: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Epidemiology of Infection — Transmission of Infection
questions.subject: Medicine

questions.question: The Gestalt law of 'proximity' states that:

options.A: Items that are close together in space or time tend to be perceived as belonging together, forming a group
options.B: Only identical items can ever be grouped together
options.C: Distant objects are always perceived as larger
options.D: Proximity has no influence on perceptual grouping

questions.explanation: The law of proximity states that items close together in space or time tend to be perceived as belonging together or forming an organized group — for example, seeing three pairs of lines rather than six separate lines when they are grouped closely.
questions.sourceBook: Morgan & King, Introduction to Psychology
questions.sourceChapter: Sensory Processes and Perception — Organization in Perception
questions.subject: Psychology

questions.question: Strokes are broadly classified into two main categories based on underlying pathology:

options.B: Acute and chronic only

questions.explanation: Strokes are broadly classified as ischemic (from thrombus, embolism, or low systemic perfusion depriving brain tissue of blood flow) or hemorrhagic (from rupture of a cerebral vessel causing bleeding into or around the brain).
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 15: Stroke — Pathophysiology
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: An 'obstructive' spirometry pattern is characterised by:

options.A: Reduction in FEV1 with relative preservation of FVC (forced vital capacity)
options.B: Simultaneous reduction of both FEV1 and FVC with an increased FEV1/FVC ratio
options.C: No change in either FEV1 or FVC
options.D: An increase in both FEV1 and FVC

questions.explanation: An obstructive pattern shows a reduction in FEV1 (forced expiratory volume in 1 second) with relative preservation of FVC, lowering the FEV1/FVC ratio — this indicates airway obstruction, graded by severity (e.g. <75% mild, <60% moderate, <40% severe). A restrictive pattern, by contrast, shows simultaneous reduction of both FEV1 and FVC with an increased ratio.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.sourceChapter: Cardiopulmonary Function Testing — Airway Function
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: The basic requirements of good epidemiological measurement include validity, reliability, accuracy, sensitivity, and:

options.B: Profitability
options.D: Simplicity above all else, regardless of accuracy

questions.explanation: The basic requirements of measurement in epidemiology are validity, reliability, accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity — these properties determine how trustworthy and useful a given measurement or test is for epidemiological purposes.
questions.sourceBook: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Epidemiology and Epidemiologic Methods — Basic Measurements in Epidemiology
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Community Health

questions.question: For a typical healthy but untrained adult beginning a resistance training program, the recommended training zone (percentage of baseline RM) generally falls between:
questions.explanation: For healthy but untrained adults, a typical training zone falls between 40% and 70% of the baseline RM, with the lower end of the range safer at the start of a program to focus on correct form before progressing intensity.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 6: Resistance Exercise — Training Zone
questions.subject: Kinesio Therapeutics

questions.question: Prepatellar bursitis is commonly known by which occupational nickname?

options.B: Tennis elbow

questions.explanation: Prepatellar bursitis is commonly called 'housemaid's knee' (or miner's knee), from repeated kneeling pressure directly on the kneecap. Subcutaneous infrapatellar bursitis, by contrast, is called 'clergyman's knee'.
questions.sourceBook: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy — Lower Limb
questions.sourceChapter: Front of Thigh — Clinical Anatomy
questions.subject: Anatomy

questions.question: 'Overconfidence bias' in clinical decision-making refers to:

options.A: The tendency to always order more diagnostic tests than necessary
options.B: The tendency to believe one knows more than one actually does, placing too much faith in opinion over gathered evidence
options.C: A bias that only affects junior doctors, never senior clinicians
options.D: Excessive reliance on clinical prediction rules

questions.explanation: Overconfidence bias is the tendency to place too much faith in one's own opinion rather than the gathered evidence, sometimes compounded further by availability bias and commission bias (a tendency to act rather than not act), occasionally with serious consequences.
questions.sourceBook: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Clinical Decision Making — Common Cognitive Biases
questions.subject: Medicine

questions.question: When testing hip abductor strength in a patient with an unstable knee, resistance is applied at the distal femur (just above the knee) instead of at the ankle. Using this shorter lever, what is the highest grade that can be assigned, even if the patient tolerates maximal resistance?

options.B: Grade 4

questions.explanation: A shorter lever (resistance near the knee rather than at the ankle) makes the test mechanically easier, so a patient who takes maximal resistance in this position can still only be graded a 4 — the longer lever at the ankle is needed to truly demonstrate Grade 5 strength, since it better reflects the functional demand of gait.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels and Worthingham's Muscle Testing, 9th ed.
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 1: Principles of Manual Muscle Testing
questions.subject: Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills

questions.question: How many carpal bones make up the wrist, and in how many rows are they arranged?

options.B: 8 bones in two rows

questions.explanation: The carpus is made up of 8 carpal bones arranged in two rows of four: a proximal row (scaphoid, lunate, triquetral, pisiform, from lateral to medial) and a distal row (trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate).
questions.sourceBook: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy — Upper Limb
questions.sourceChapter: Bones of the Upper Limb — Carpal Bones
questions.subject: Anatomy

questions.question: Anterior Cerebral Artery (ACA) syndrome classically produces contralateral hemiparesis and sensory loss that is:

options.A: Greater in the lower extremity than the upper extremity
options.B: Greater in the upper extremity and face than the lower extremity
options.C: Equal throughout the whole body with no distinguishing pattern

questions.explanation: Because the ACA supplies the medial aspect of the cerebral hemisphere where the lower extremity is somatotopically represented, ACA syndrome classically produces contralateral hemiparesis and sensory loss with greater involvement of the lower extremity than the upper extremity — the opposite pattern to MCA syndrome.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 15: Stroke — Anterior Cerebral Artery Syndrome
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: A 'repetition maximum' (RM), as first described by DeLorme, is defined as:

options.A: The greatest amount of weight a muscle can move through full available ROM a specific number of times before fatiguing
options.B: The maximum number of exercise sessions a patient can complete in a week
options.C: The total duration in months of a resistance training program
options.D: A measure of joint range of motion only

questions.explanation: A repetition maximum (RM) is the greatest amount of weight (load) a muscle can move through the full available range of motion, with control, a specific number of times before fatiguing — e.g. a '10-RM' is the maximum weight that can be lifted through 10 repetitions.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 6: Resistance Exercise — Repetition Maximum
questions.subject: Kinesio Therapeutics

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: Impulses with a duration of less than 10 ms, used for stimulating normal (innervated) muscle, are classified as having:

options.A: A long duration, termed interrupted direct current
options.B: A short duration, of the faradic type
options.C: No classification exists for pulse duration
options.D: A duration only used for denervated muscle

questions.explanation: Impulses of less than 10 ms duration are classed as short duration and are of the faradic type, used to stimulate normal innervated muscle via its motor nerve, typically repeated at a high rate of 50-100 per second.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: The acronym TORCH, used for a group of congenital infections with overlapping symptoms, stands for Toxoplasma, Others, Rubella, Cytomegalovirus, and:

options.B: Hepatitis A virus

questions.explanation: TORCH stands for Toxoplasma, Others (hepatitis B, coxsackievirus B, mumps, poliovirus), Rubella, Cytomegalovirus, and Herpes simplex virus — a group of infections tested together in suspected congenital infection because their symptoms in the newborn are often indistinguishable from one another.
questions.sourceBook: Harsh Mohan, Textbook of Pathology
questions.sourceChapter: Infectious and Parasitic Diseases — TORCH Complex
questions.subject: Pathology & Microbiology

questions.question: To achieve full passive range of hip flexion, the knee must also be allowed to flex. Why?

options.A: It relaxes tension on the two-joint hamstring muscle group, which would otherwise restrict hip flexion
options.B: It reduces pain in the lumbar spine
options.C: It is required purely to stabilize the pelvis
options.D: Knee position has no real effect on hip flexion range

questions.explanation: The hamstrings cross both the hip and knee. Keeping the knee extended while flexing the hip stretches the hamstrings and limits how far the hip can flex; flexing the knee releases that tension, allowing full hip flexion range to be reached.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 3: Range of Motion — Combined Hip and Knee Motion
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Exercise Therapy

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: As the frequency of repeated electrical stimuli to a motor nerve increases beyond about 20 Hz, what happens to the muscle's contraction pattern?

options.B: There is no longer time for complete relaxation between contractions, producing partial tetany
options.C: Contraction strength decreases progressively to zero
options.D: The muscle contracts only once regardless of how many stimuli are given

questions.explanation: At low stimulation frequencies (e.g. 1 per second), each stimulus produces an isolated twitch with complete relaxation between contractions. As frequency increases, the relaxation period shortens; beyond about 20 Hz there is no longer time for complete relaxation between contractions, producing partial tetany.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle — Effects of Frequency of Stimulation
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: A binding site that attaches a drug but produces no pharmacological response at all (e.g. many plasma protein binding sites) is best termed a:

options.B: Silent receptor (or drug acceptor / site of loss)

questions.explanation: Sites that bind a drug without producing any response are called silent receptors, or more accurately drug acceptors / sites of loss — the term 'receptor' is best reserved for binding sites capable of generating an actual biological response.
questions.sourceBook: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology
questions.sourceChapter: Mechanism of Drug Action; Receptor Pharmacology
questions.subject: Pharmacology

questions.question: In the Active Compression Test of O'Brien, pain that is present with the arm pronated (thumb down) but reduced or eliminated with the arm supinated (thumb up) suggests a positive test for:

options.B: A simple rotator cuff strain with no labral involvement

questions.explanation: O'Brien's active compression test is positive for a superior labral injury when pain (felt 'inside' the shoulder, not at the AC joint) is produced with the arm pronated, and is reduced or eliminated when the same maneuver is repeated with the arm supinated.
questions.sourceBook: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 5: Shoulder — Active Compression Test of O'Brien
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: Pleuritic chest pain is best described as:

options.A: A dull, central, band-like pain radiating to the jaw
options.B: A severe, sharp, stabbing pain, worse on inspiration, and not reproduced by palpation
options.C: A burning retrosternal pain worse when lying flat or bending forward
options.D: Pain that is only ever felt during exercise and never at rest

questions.explanation: Pleuritic chest pain, from inflammation of the parietal pleura, is classically a severe, sharp, stabbing pain that worsens on inspiration and is NOT reproduced by palpation — distinguishing it from musculoskeletal chest wall pain, which IS reproduced by palpation.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.sourceChapter: Assessment — Chest Pain
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: Which carpal bone is described as the largest, with a rounded head, occupying the centre of the distal row?

options.B: Trapezoid

questions.explanation: The capitate is the largest carpal bone, identified by its rounded head, and sits in the distal row.
questions.sourceBook: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy — Upper Limb
questions.sourceChapter: Bones of the Upper Limb — Carpal Bones
questions.subject: Anatomy

questions.question: By definition, a transient ischemic attack (TIA) produces focal neurological deficits that:

options.A: Last longer than 24 hours with permanent residual damage
options.B: Do not last longer than 24 hours, with no evidence of residual brain damage afterward
options.C: Always progress to a completed stroke within 24 hours
options.D: Only ever affect vision, never motor function

questions.explanation: A TIA is a temporary interruption of blood supply producing focal neurological deficits lasting minutes to hours but, by definition, not longer than 24 hours, with no evidence of residual damage afterward. However, TIA is clinically significant as a warning sign — about 15% of strokes are preceded by a TIA, with the highest risk in the following 90 days.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 15: Stroke — Management Categories
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: The 'unpacking principle' in clinical reasoning refers to the risk that:

options.A: A failure to fully take the history and examine the patient means important information can be missed, leading to error
options.B: Patients should always be admitted for observation regardless of findings
options.C: Clinical prediction rules should never be used
options.D: Diagnostic tests are always more reliable than clinical examination

questions.explanation: The unpacking principle highlights that history-taking and physical examination, though seemingly obvious steps, are sometimes performed inadequately — and this failure to 'unpack' all the available information can cause important findings to be missed.
questions.sourceBook: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Clinical Decision Making — Reducing Errors, Cognitive Debiasing Strategies
questions.subject: Medicine

questions.question: A 'restrictive' spirometry pattern, usually associated with reduced lung volume, is characterised by:

options.A: Simultaneous reduction of both FEV1 and FVC, with an INCREASED FEV1/FVC ratio
options.B: Reduction in FEV1 only, with FVC completely unaffected
options.C: No change in spirometry values at all
options.D: An increased FVC with a normal FEV1

questions.explanation: A restrictive pattern shows simultaneous reduction of both FEV1 and FVC together, with an increased FEV1/FVC ratio (since the lungs are small and empty quickly) — distinct from the obstructive pattern where FEV1 drops disproportionately more than FVC.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.sourceChapter: Cardiopulmonary Function Testing — Airway Function
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: Impulses with a duration of MORE than 10 ms, often termed interrupted (or modified) direct current, are specifically used to stimulate:

options.A: Normal, innervated muscle via the motor nerve
options.B: Denervated muscle, where the muscle fibres must be stimulated directly (no functioning motor nerve)

questions.explanation: Long-duration impulses (>10 ms), termed interrupted or modified direct current, are used for denervated muscles — since there is no functioning motor nerve, the muscle fibres must be stimulated directly, and these impulses are repeated far less frequently than faradic-type currents (e.g. a 100 ms impulse might be repeated only about 30 times per minute).
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SH) typically results from rupture of which type of vascular lesion?

options.A: A saccular (berry) aneurysm affecting large blood vessels
options.B: Small penetrating vessel disease (lacunar disease)
options.C: Atherosclerotic plaque in the carotid artery only
options.D: Venous thrombosis in the dural sinuses exclusively

questions.explanation: Subarachnoid hemorrhage typically occurs from bleeding into the subarachnoid space, most often from rupture of a saccular (berry) aneurysm affecting the larger cerebral blood vessels, often related to congenital weakness in the vessel wall.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 15: Stroke — Pathophysiology
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: The normal platelet count in circulating blood is approximately:

options.B: 1,000 per microlitre
options.D: Platelets have no measurable normal range

questions.explanation: The normal platelet count is approximately 1.5 to 4 lakhs (150,000 to 400,000) per microlitre, with an average around 2.5 lakhs/microlitre, and remains quite constant under normal conditions.
questions.sourceBook: AK Jain, Physiology
questions.sourceChapter: Platelets or Thrombocytes — Count and Variations
questions.subject: Physiology

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: Faradic-type currents are typically 'surged' for treatment purposes. What is the purpose of surging the current?

options.A: To reduce the total treatment time
options.B: To produce a near-normal tetanic-like contraction and relaxation of the muscle, by gradually increasing then decreasing the intensity of successive impulses
options.C: To eliminate the need for any electrodes
options.D: To convert the current into direct current permanently

questions.explanation: Surging gradually increases the intensity of successive impulses to a peak, then lets it fall (suddenly or gradually), mimicking a more natural, near-normal tetanic muscle contraction and relaxation cycle rather than an abrupt on/off stimulus.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle — Modified Faradic Currents
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: For the vertebroscapular muscles (e.g., the rhomboids), resistance is preferably applied on the arm rather than directly on the scapula, their true point of insertion. Why?

options.A: It is simply easier for the therapist to grip the arm
options.B: The longer lever at the arm better reflects the functional demand of controlling the weight of the whole upper limb
options.C: The scapula moves too unpredictably to resist against
options.D: Resistance at the scapula risks skin breakdown

questions.explanation: Applying resistance on the arm uses a longer lever that more closely reflects the functional load these muscles must control (the weight of the arm), rather than testing at their literal anatomical insertion.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels and Worthingham's Muscle Testing, 9th ed.
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 1: Principles of Manual Muscle Testing
questions.subject: Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills

questions.question: Malignant tumours arising from epithelial tissue are generally named:

options.B: Carcinomas

questions.explanation: Malignant tumours of epithelial origin are called carcinomas, while malignant tumours of mesenchymal (connective tissue) origin are called sarcomas.
questions.sourceBook: Harsh Mohan, Textbook of Pathology
questions.sourceChapter: Neoplasia — Nomenclature and Classification
questions.subject: Pathology & Microbiology

questions.question: Corticosteroid therapy (e.g. methylprednisolone) used to treat acute MS relapses primarily works to:

options.B: Shorten the duration of the acute exacerbation through anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effects, without modifying the overall disease course
options.C: Cure the underlying autoimmune process entirely
options.D: Have no measurable clinical effect on relapses

questions.explanation: Corticosteroids like methylprednisolone reduce inflammation and suppress immune activity, shortening the duration of an acute relapse — but they do NOT modify the overall disease course or degree of long-term recovery.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 16: Multiple Sclerosis — Management of Acute Relapses
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: When an electrical current stimulates a nerve fibre, the surface of the plasma membrane nearer the cathode becomes:

options.B: More negative relative to the opposite surface, which can reduce the resting potential difference across the membrane on the cathode side and initiate an impulse if it falls enough for sodium permeability to increase
options.D: Permanently depolarised with no possibility of returning to rest

questions.explanation: The membrane surface nearer the cathode becomes more negative. On the side of the nerve nearer the cathode, this additional charge is of opposite polarity to the resting membrane potential, reducing the potential difference (PD) across it — if the PD falls enough for the membrane to become permeable to sodium ions, an impulse is initiated.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle — Mechanism of Nerve Stimulation
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: Sharrard's postmortem motor neuron counts in poliomyelitis patients, cited in Daniels and Worthingham, found that by the time a muscle's MMT grade had fallen to 4 (Good), approximately what proportion of its motor neurons were already lost?

options.B: About 25%

questions.explanation: Sharrard's data showed that more than half of a muscle's motor neurons were already gone by the time its MMT grade dropped to 4, which is why the text emphasizes that a 'Good' muscle already represents real, clinically significant weakness.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels and Worthingham's Muscle Testing, 9th ed.
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 1: Principles of Manual Muscle Testing
questions.subject: Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills

questions.question: In prolonged fasting (beyond 48-72 hours), the central nervous system adapts to using which fuel source as primary, reducing the need for muscle protein breakdown?

options.B: Dietary fibre

questions.explanation: After 48-72 hours of fasting, the CNS adapts to using ketone bodies (produced by hepatic ketogenesis from fatty acids, facilitated by low insulin) as its primary fuel source — this 'fat fuel economy' shift reduces the need for muscle breakdown by up to 55 g per day compared to simple short-term starvation.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Nutrition and Fluid Therapy — Metabolic Response to Starvation
questions.subject: General Surgery & Orthopedics

questions.question: Lipofuscin, sometimes called the 'wear and tear pigment', is most characteristically associated with:

options.B: Atrophied cells in ageing (e.g. 'brown atrophy' of the heart)

questions.explanation: Lipofuscin is a golden-brown intralysosomal pigment that accumulates in atrophied cells of old age (hence 'wear and tear pigment'), seen in myocardial fibres (producing 'brown atrophy' of the heart), hepatocytes, and neurons in senile dementia.
questions.sourceBook: Harsh Mohan, Textbook of Pathology
questions.sourceChapter: Cell Injury, Cellular Adaptations and Cellular Ageing — Lipofuscin
questions.subject: Pathology & Microbiology

questions.question: In epidemiological studies, 'comparability' between study and control groups is best ensured by:

options.A: Choosing groups of very different ages and backgrounds to maximise contrast
options.B: Randomization or random allocation, or 'matching' for selected characteristics when random allocation is not possible (e.g. case-control/cohort studies)
options.C: Always excluding any consideration of age or sex
options.D: Comparability is not actually necessary for valid epidemiological conclusions

questions.explanation: Comparability ('like being compared with like') between study and control groups is best ensured by randomization or random allocation. Where this is not possible, such as in case-control or cohort studies, 'matching' for selected characteristics is used instead, and standardization can address a limited number of characteristics like age, sex, and parity.
questions.sourceBook: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Epidemiology and Epidemiologic Methods — Making Comparisons
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Community Health

questions.question: Unwanted but often unavoidable pharmacodynamic effects that occur at normal therapeutic doses, and are generally predictable from a drug's known pharmacological profile, are classified as:

options.B: Side effects

questions.explanation: Side effects are unwanted but often unavoidable pharmacodynamic effects occurring at therapeutic doses — generally not serious, predictable from the drug's pharmacological profile, and often improved by reducing the dose (e.g. dry mouth from atropine's antisecretory action).
questions.sourceBook: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology
questions.sourceChapter: Adverse Drug Effects — Classification
questions.subject: Pharmacology

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: When beginning faradic stimulation of a muscle group, what is the recommended approach to intensity?

options.A: Start immediately at maximal tolerable intensity
options.B: Give several gentle contractions first to allow the patient to become accustomed to the current, then gradually increase intensity
options.C: Intensity should never be increased throughout the treatment
options.D: Intensity is irrelevant to the treatment outcome

questions.explanation: The recommended approach is to give the patient several gentle contractions first to allow them to become accustomed to the current, then gradually increase the intensity until a strong contraction is achieved — not starting at a high, potentially uncomfortable intensity immediately.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Stimulation of Muscle Groups — Quadriceps
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: How long should postpartum exercises generally be continued for maximal benefit, per standard obstetric guidance?

options.A: Only for the first 24 hours after delivery
options.B: At least 3 months
options.C: Only once, on the day of discharge
options.D: Postpartum exercise is not recommended at all

questions.explanation: Postpartum exercises — breathing exercises, leg movements, and toning of abdominal, pelvic floor, and back muscles — should be continued for at least 3 months, and are ideally taught by a trained physiotherapist.
questions.sourceBook: Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics
questions.sourceChapter: Normal Puerperium — Postpartum Exercise
questions.subject: OBGY

questions.question: Which special test is specifically associated with assessing patellofemoral (patellar) instability?

options.B: McMurray test

questions.explanation: The apprehension test is used to assess for patellar instability — the examiner laterally displaces the patella and observes for a look or feeling of apprehension from the patient, who fears the patella is about to dislocate.
questions.sourceBook: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: At what approximate stimulation frequency does a muscle contraction become fully tetanic, with no perceptible relaxation between successive contractions?

options.B: Under 1 Hz
options.D: Frequency has no relationship to tetany

questions.explanation: As stimulation frequency increases beyond 20 Hz, partial tetany develops; further increases progressively reduce relaxation until, at frequencies over 60 Hz, there is no perceptible relaxation between contractions and the response is fully tetanic.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle — Effects of Frequency of Stimulation
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: Two-joint muscles such as the hamstrings and gastrocnemius are typically tested in mid-range rather than at full end-range during manual muscle testing. Why?

options.A: To avoid provoking a stretch reflex
options.B: Mid-range gives these muscles a more mechanically favorable length-tension relationship for the test
options.C: Two-joint muscles cannot generate any force at end range
options.D: It standardizes the time taken for every muscle test

questions.explanation: One-joint muscles are tested at end range for consistency, but two-joint muscles are tested in mid-range, where their length-tension relationship is more favorable — testing them at a mechanical disadvantage would make it hard to distinguish a true Grade 5 from a Grade 4.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels and Worthingham's Muscle Testing, 9th ed.
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 1: Principles of Manual Muscle Testing
questions.subject: Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills

questions.question: The unique sequence of amino acids in a protein, determined by the genes in DNA, is called its:

options.B: Primary structure

questions.explanation: The primary structure of a protein is its specific linear sequence of amino acids, determined by the genetic code. It is largely responsible for the protein's function, and a large number of genetic diseases arise from abnormalities in this amino acid sequence.
questions.sourceBook: Satyanarayana, Biochemistry
questions.sourceChapter: Proteins and Amino Acids — Primary Structure
questions.subject: Biochemistry

questions.question: Orchidopexy for a palpable undescended testis is ideally performed at what age, to optimise fertility outcomes?

options.B: Between 6 and 12 months of age
options.D: Age has no bearing on fertility outcomes

questions.explanation: Orchidopexy is ideally performed as a day-case procedure between 6 and 12 months of age. Bringing the testis into the scrotum (below core body temperature) at a young age optimises spermatogenesis and fertility outcomes.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Paediatric Surgery — Undescended Testes

questions.question: The ABCDE approach (Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure) used in critically ill patients is an example of which error-reduction strategy?

options.B: A mnemonic/checklist

questions.explanation: ABCDE is probably the most widely used mnemonic/checklist in medicine, reducing reliance on fallible memory and ensuring important issues are considered systematically, especially under stress, complexity, or fatigue.
questions.sourceBook: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Clinical Decision Making — Mnemonics and Checklists

questions.question: Which of the following is a documented benefit of Continuous Passive Motion (CPM) following joint surgery?

options.A: A permanent increase in muscle strength
options.B: Increased synovial fluid lubrication and a stimulating effect on healing of cartilage, tendons, and ligaments
options.C: It removes the need for any active exercise afterward

questions.explanation: Documented benefits of CPM include increased synovial fluid lubrication (supporting cartilage healing), a stimulating effect on tendon and ligament healing, prevention of adhesions/contractures, and typically a quicker return of range of motion with less postoperative pain — but it does not replace active exercise or strength training.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 3: Range of Motion — Continuous Passive Motion
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Exercise Therapy

questions.question: Breathlessness specifically occurring when a patient lies flat is termed:

options.B: Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea

questions.explanation: Orthopnoea is breathlessness specifically triggered by lying flat, classically because it increases venous return from the legs, causing blood to pool in the lungs in cardiac patients. Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea (PND) is a related but distinct pattern — breathlessness that wakes the patient from sleep at night.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.sourceChapter: Assessment — Breathlessness

questions.question: A pregnant woman with a history of four or more previous births is termed:

options.B: Primipara

questions.explanation: A woman with a previous history of four or more births is called a grand multipara — distinct from nullipara (never completed a pregnancy to viability) and primipara (has delivered exactly one viable child).
questions.sourceBook: Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics
questions.sourceChapter: Antenatal Care — History Taking, Terminology

questions.question: On the International Death Certificate, the 'underlying cause of death' is recorded in Part I, and is defined as:

options.A: The immediate mode of dying, such as 'heart failure' or 'asthenia'
options.B: The disease or injury that initiated the chain of morbid events leading directly to death, or the circumstances of the accident/violence that produced the fatal injury
options.C: Any condition present at death regardless of its role in causing it
options.D: Only conditions diagnosed after an autopsy

questions.explanation: The underlying cause of death is the disease or injury that initiated the train of morbid events leading directly to death, or the circumstances of the accident/violence producing the fatal injury — the certificate explicitly notes this does NOT mean the immediate mode of dying (e.g. 'heart failure' or 'asthenia' are not acceptable as the underlying cause).
questions.sourceBook: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Measurement of Mortality — International Death Certificate
